h1: Bobek hops in English bitters and Belgian ales
title: Bobek Hops in Bitters and Belgian Ales | Craft Beer School
desc: Bobek hops explained: the Slovenian variety, its gentle earthy and spicy aroma, how to use it in bitters and Belgian ales and a 20 litre bitter recipe.
teaser: Bobek is a Slovenian hop with an earthy, spicy, quietly fruity character. It sits well in old-fashioned malt-led beers.
standfirst: Bobek is a Slovenian hop that is less loud than American varieties and more useful for it. Here is how it behaves and where it belongs.
sections:
Bobek is a hop variety from Slovenia, grown in the Savinja valley, where the country's main hop gardens lie. Slovenian hops grew up in the European tradition of noble and Styrian types: moderate alpha acid, low to moderate oil and gentle, earthy aroma.

Bobek is usually described as earthy and herbal with a touch of spice and mild citrus. Alpha acid is in the middle single digits, so it is happy at the start of the boil as well as the end. It is a quiet, supporting hop, not a showpiece.

A bitter is a malt-led beer with moderate strength, often around 3.5 to 5% ABV. The hops frame the malt rather than shouting over it. A traditional bitter wants a firm, clean bitterness with a little earthy or floral aroma. Bobek provides that without the citrus and resin of an American hop.

It also pairs with the robust character of English varieties. Our English hops guide compares the family. The notes on Challenger and Target show the bittering options you can pair with Bobek for flavour.

This recipe aims for an original gravity near 1.043, about 25 IBU and 4.2% ABV. Adjust the grain bill to your own efficiency.

  • Maris Otter pale malt 3.4 kg (85%).
  • Crystal malt around 120 EBC 0.4 kg (10%).
  • Torrefied wheat 0.2 kg (5%).
  • Target 15 g at 60 minutes.
  • Bobek 20 g at 10 minutes.
  • Bobek 20 g at flameout.

Mash at 66 to 67 °C for 60 minutes. Ferment with an English ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. Aim for a final gravity near 1.011. Serve at cellar temperature, around 10 to 13 °C, to let the malt and hops show.

The balance is worth checking. Bitterness units divided by the gravity points (43 here) gives about 0.6, a typical figure for a bitter. A ratio far below that tastes sweet and soft. Far above and the beer turns harsh, especially with the crystal malt in the mix.

Belgian blonde and pale ales rely on yeast for much of their character: fruity esters, a hint of spice and a dry finish. The hops stay in the background. Bobek's mild spice and herbal edge sit comfortably alongside that yeast character without competing.

A Belgian blonde might use pilsner malt with a little sugar to keep the body light, a modest bitterness of 20 to 25 IBU and Bobek late in the boil. Ferment warmer than for a bitter, around 20 to 24 °C. Let the yeast flavour show. Control the temperature, because a Belgian yeast pushed too high produces harsh solvent notes.

Bobek is a specialist hop and not widely stocked, so plan ahead. Pellets from a European supplier arrive sealed. Keep them in the freezer and use them within a season. Moderate-oil hops lose their quiet aroma easily in warm storage. If you cannot find Bobek, a small blend of Styrian Goldings and a Fuggle-type hop gets near the earthy, spicy profile.

In a hot city, bitters have an advantage. They are brewed at ale temperatures. Moderate gravity makes them easier to drink in the heat than a heavy stout. Serve them cool, not ice cold. A pint of bitter on a warm evening is a very different drink from a pint of chilled lager. That difference is the point. Let the glass sit in your hand for a minute and the malt opens up.
Getting the most out of a gentle hop

Gentle hops reward restraint. Do not dry hop heavily, because the aroma is subtle and a big charge can add grassy notes. A short stand in the whirlpool or a late boil addition is enough. Taste a pint at the end of conditioning and decide whether the hop needs more or less next time.

One change at a time is the rule. If you change the hop, the yeast and the mash in one batch, you cannot tell what did what.
A hop like Bobek rewards a brewer who knows about oils and how they survive. That knowledge lets you choose and place any hop with confidence, rather than waiting for someone to publish a recipe.
faqs: Earthy and herbal with a touch of spice and mild citrus. It is a quiet hop that supports malt.
Is Bobek a bittering or aroma hop?
It has moderate alpha acid, so it can do either. Most brewers use it late for flavour and combine it with a firmer bittering hop.
English bitters, golden ales and Belgian blonde or pale ales, where the hop supports malt and yeast.
A blend of Styrian Goldings and a Fuggle-type hop is the nearest in profile. Taste and adjust.
